title: LRU Cache — HashMap + doubly linked list, O(1) get/put.
shortTitle: LRU Cache — HashMap plus doubly linked list for O(1) get and put

s1_definition.profdef: An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the least recently accessed entry when it is full. The classic O(1) design combines a hash map, which gives constant-time lookup from a key to its node, with a doubly linked list, which maintains usage order so the most recently used entry sits at one end and the least recently used sits at the other, allowing both get and put to run in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India teller keeps only the twenty most recently touched customer files on the desk because space is limited. Every time a file is read or updated, it moves to the front of the pile. When a brand new file arrives and the desk is full, the file at the very back, the one nobody has touched in the longest time, is put back in the archive. The desk is the cache, the pile order is the linked list, and a quick index of where each file sits is the hash map.
s1_definition.oneliner: A hash map finds the node instantly and a doubly linked list reorders it instantly, so every get and put touches the entry and promotes it to most-recently-used in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the least recently accessed entry when it is full. The classic O(1) design combines a hash map, which gives constant-time lookup from a key to its node, with a doubly linked list, which maintains usage order so the most recently used entry sits at one end and the least recently used sits at the other, allowing both get and put to run in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India teller keeps only the twenty most recently touched customer files on the desk because space is limited. Every time a file is read or updated, it moves to the front of the pile. When a brand new file arrives and the desk is full, the file at the very back, the one nobody has touched in the longest time, is put back in the archive. The desk is the cache, the pile order is the linked list, and a quick index of where each file sits is the hash map.

**One line to remember:** A hash map finds the node instantly and a doubly linked list reorders it instantly, so every get and put touches the entry and promotes it to most-recently-used in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The cache has a fixed capacity. Internally it keeps a hash map from key to a node object, and a doubly linked list of those nodes. Each node holds the key, the value, and pointers to the previous and next nodes. I keep two sentinel nodes, a head and a tail, so that inserting and removing never need null checks at the ends.

A `get(key)` looks up the node in the map. If absent, it returns a miss. If present, it reads the value, removes the node from its current position in the list, and reinserts it right after the head, marking it most recently used. Both the removal and reinsertion are constant time because a doubly linked list node knows its neighbors.

A `put(key, value)` checks the map. If the key exists, it updates the value and moves the node to the front. If the key is new, it creates a node, inserts it at the front, and stores it in the map. If adding it exceeds capacity, it removes the node just before the tail, which is the least recently used entry, and also deletes that key from the map.

The head side represents most recently used and the tail side represents least recently used. Using sentinel head and tail nodes removes edge cases for an empty list or single element. The whole structure gives O(1) average time for both operations because the map avoids scanning and the linked list avoids shifting.

A senior nuance: you must remove the evicted key from the map as well as from the list, otherwise the map leaks memory and later lookups find stale nodes. Another nuance is that in Java you could reach for `LinkedHashMap` with access order and an overridden `removeEldestEntry`, but implementing the map plus doubly linked list by hand demonstrates the mechanics interviewers want to see.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's account service answers millions of balance lookups. Hitting the database every time is slow, so hot accounts are cached in memory, but memory is finite and only the most active accounts should stay cached.

This is exactly how an LRU cache works. The most recently accessed accounts stay, and the stalest one is evicted when the cache fills.

Problem 2 — Both reading a cached balance and updating it must be fast and must also mark that account as freshly used, so a frequently checked account is never evicted just because a burst of other lookups happened.

This is exactly why we combine a hash map for instant lookup with a doubly linked list for instant reordering, so every access promotes the account to most recently used in constant time.

The code will have an `Account`-flavored key-value usage, a `LruCache` class backed by a hash map and a hand-built doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail, a `Node` class, and a runnable demo that fills the cache, triggers an eviction, and logs hits, misses, and evictions.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cache of capacity 2, then a sequence of puts and gets.

Step 1: `put("SAV2001", 1000000)` creates a node for Rajesh and places it right after the head. The map now holds one entry and the list order from head to tail is Rajesh then tail.

Step 2: `put("CUR3001", 250000)` creates Priya's node at the front. The order from head to tail is now Priya, Rajesh, tail. Rajesh is the least recently used.

Step 3: `get("SAV2001")` finds Rajesh in the map, reads 1000000, removes his node and reinserts it at the front. The order becomes Rajesh, Priya, tail. Now Priya is least recently used.

Step 4: `put("SAV4002", 75000)` is a new key, so a node is added at the front and the map size becomes three, exceeding capacity. The node before the tail, Priya, is removed from the list and her key is deleted from the map and logged as an eviction.

Step 5: `get("CUR3001")` now misses because Priya was evicted. `get("SAV2001")` and `get("SAV4002")` both hit.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get SAV2001 -> 1000000
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    EVICT CUR3001
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get CUR3001 -> null
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get SAV2001 -> 1000000
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get SAV4002 -> 75000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  put SAV2001, put CUR3001        list (head→tail): [CUR3001][SAV2001]
    │                              map: {SAV2001, CUR3001}
    ▼
  get SAV2001 (HIT)              moveToFront(SAV2001)
    │                              list: [SAV2001][CUR3001]
    ▼
  put SAV4002 (NEW)             addFront → size 3 > cap 2
    │                              evict tail.prev = CUR3001
    │                              remove from list AND map
    ▼
  list: [SAV4002][SAV2001]      map: {SAV4002, SAV2001}
    │
    ├─ get CUR3001 → MISS (null)
    └─ get SAV2001 / SAV4002 → HIT
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — LruCache ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns / Principles ───────────────────────────┐
  │  HashMap for O(1) lookup + Doubly Linked List for order  │
  │  Sentinel head/tail nodes remove edge cases              │
  │  S (SOLID): LruCache only caches with LRU policy         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │          LruCache             │ owns  │      Node        │
  │  - capacity: int              │◆─────▶│  + key: String   │
  │  - map: Map<String,Node>      │       │  + value: long   │
  │  - head: Node (MRU sentinel)  │       │  + prev: Node    │
  │  - tail: Node (LRU sentinel)  │       │  + next: Node    │
  │  ─────────────────────────────│       └──────────────────┘
  │  + get(key): Long             │  O(1)
  │  + put(key, value): void      │  O(1)
  │  - addFront/remove/moveToFront│
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for put:
    Post: size never exceeds capacity; evicted key removed from BOTH list and map
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An LRU cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that, when it runs out of room, evicts the entry that was accessed least recently. The design that interviewers want is the one that makes both get and put run in constant time, and I achieve that by combining two data structures: a hash map that maps each key to a node for instant lookup, and a doubly linked list that keeps the nodes ordered by how recently they were used.

The linked list has a most-recently-used end and a least-recently-used end, and I always keep two sentinel nodes, a head and a tail, so that inserting and removing at the ends never require special null handling. On a get, I find the node through the map, read its value, and move it to the front to mark it most recently used. On a put, if the key exists I update the value and move it to the front, and if the key is new I create a node at the front and store it in the map; if that pushes the size over capacity, I remove the node just before the tail, which is the least recently used, and I also delete its key from the map.

The detail that separates a correct implementation from a leaky one is that when I evict, I must remove the key from the hash map as well as from the linked list. If I only unlink it from the list, the map keeps a stale reference and the cache slowly leaks memory while reporting a wrong size. I also mention that Java offers LinkedHashMap with access order and a removeEldestEntry hook as a shortcut, but building the map plus doubly linked list by hand shows I actually understand the mechanics.

In my project at National Bank of India, the account service answered millions of balance lookups, and hitting the database every time was too slow, so we cached the hottest accounts in memory with an LRU policy. The hash map plus doubly linked list gave constant-time reads and writes, and promoting an account to most recently used on every access meant a frequently checked account was never evicted just because a burst of unrelated lookups came through, which kept our cache hit rate high and the database load low.
